primer.ind_p_world.title: Hindustan
primer.ind_p_world.text: You were born in Hindustan, as Persians and Turks call the lands beyond the Indus. There is no single country: in the north rule the sultans of Delhi, who came from Afghanistan and Central Asia; in the south, Hindu rajas; on the coasts, sultans and princes of their own. Over these four centuries the Delhi Sultanate will pass through five dynasties, the empire of Vijayanagara will rise in the south, and in 1526 the Mughals will arrive. More than a hundred million people live here, nearly all of them in villages.
primer.ind_p_world_mamluk.title: The Slave Sultans
primer.ind_p_world_mamluk.text: You were born under the first sultans of Delhi. In 1192 Muhammad of Ghor defeated Raja Prithviraj Chauhan, and in 1206 his former slave soldier, Qutb ud-Din Aibak, became the first sultan. That is why this line is called the 'Slave dynasty': Iltutmish and Balban also began as slaves. From 1236 to 1240 Sultan Razia reigned – she rode an elephant dressed in men's clothes. Again and again the Mongols raid from the northwest.
primer.ind_p_world_khalji.title: Khaljis and Tughluqs
primer.ind_p_world_khalji.text: You were born under mighty and stern sultans. Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) beat back the Mongols, fixed prices in the markets of Delhi and sent armies to the far south. In 1327 Muhammad bin Tughluq ordered the whole capital to move a thousand kilometres to Daulatabad and tried to replace silver with copper tokens – both schemes failed. Under him the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta served as a judge in Delhi. In 1398 Timur will sack the city.
primer.ind_p_world_lodi.title: Sayyids and Lodis
primer.ind_p_world_lodi.text: You were born as the Delhi Sultanate weakens: after Timur's raid Gujarat, Malwa and Jaunpur broke away, and Delhi is ruled by the Sayyids, then from 1451 by the Afghan Lodi clan. In 1504 Sultan Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra on the Yamuna. In Mewar the Rajputs of Rana Sanga grow strong. And in Kabul Babur, a descendant of Timur, is already eyeing India – in 1526 he will come with cannon.
primer.ind_p_world_mughal.title: The Great Mughals
primer.ind_p_world_mughal.text: You were born under the Mughals. In 1526 Babur, with cannon and muskets, defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat. In 1540 his son Humayun was driven out by the Afghan Sher Shah Sur, who in five years built roads and began minting the silver rupee. Humayun returned only in 1555, and since 1556 his son Akbar has reigned, crowned at thirteen. Akbar abolished the poll tax on non-Muslims and is building the city of Fatehpur Sikri.
primer.ind_p_world_vijayanagara.title: City of Victory
primer.ind_p_world_vijayanagara.text: You were born in the empire of Vijayanagara. It was founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka, and its capital on the Tungabhadra River soon became one of the largest cities in the world. Its great rival is the Muslim Bahmani Sultanate to the north, and later the five Deccan sultanates it split into. The greatest king was Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529), poet and general. In 1565 the sultans crushed the imperial army at Talikota and sacked the capital; the kings moved to Penukonda.
primer.ind_p_world_bengal.title: Sultans of Bengal
primer.ind_p_world_bengal.text: You were born in Bengal, which has a history of its own. Around 1204 Bakhtiyar Khalji's horsemen burst into Nadia and Raja Lakshmana Sena fled. From 1352 Ilyas Shah united the land into an independent sultanate with capitals at Pandua and Gaur. Sultan Husain Shah (1494–1519) was a patron of poets writing in Bengali. More and more people embrace Islam, especially in the east, where forests are cleared for rice fields. In 1538 Sher Shah took Gaur, and in 1576 the Mughals conquered Bengal.
primer.ind_p_world_gujarat.title: Sultans of Gujarat
primer.ind_p_world_gujarat.text: You were born in Gujarat. Until 1299 Rajput kings of the Vaghela line ruled here, until the armies of Alauddin Khalji conquered the land. In 1407 the governor Zafar Khan declared himself sultan, and his grandson Ahmad Shah founded Ahmedabad in 1411. Sultan Mahmud Begada (1458–1511) was famed for his campaigns – and, legend says, for an astonishing appetite. From 1509 the Portuguese fight off Diu, and in 1573 Akbar took the land.
primer.ind_p_society.title: Varna and Jati
primer.ind_p_society.text: Sacred texts divide people into four varnas: Brahmin priests, Kshatriya warriors, Vaishya traders and farmers, Shudra labourers. In daily life jati matters more – hundreds of hereditary communities: potters, weavers, Kayastha scribes, herders. You marry within your jati, eat with it and turn to it for protection. At the bottom are those deemed 'untouchable': everyone needs their work, yet they are shunned. How strict the rules were varied from region to region. Muslims live by their own customs, but among them too, nobles of foreign descent rank themselves above converts.
primer.ind_p_society_slave.title: Bonded Servants
primer.ind_p_society_slave.text: You were born to a family of bonded servants. People fall into bondage as captives after campaigns, through debt, or in famine, when parents sell their children. Slaves are sold in the markets of Delhi, and Sultan Firuz Shah owned 180,000 of them, according to his chronicler. Slaves work in households, workshops and the army. Yet slavery here is not always a life sentence: the first sultans of Delhi – Aibak, Iltutmish, Balban – all began as slaves.
primer.ind_p_society_peasant.title: Raiyats
primer.ind_p_society_peasant.text: You were born to a family of raiyats, tillers of the soil. Everything depends on the monsoon: if the summer rains come on time there will be rice, millet and cotton; if not, famine. A share of the harvest goes in tax – Alauddin Khalji demanded half. The village is run by a headman and an accountant, the patwari, while the smith, the potter and the barber each receive a share of grain from every household. Water for the fields is raised from wells by the 'Persian wheel', a chain of clay pots turned by oxen.
primer.ind_p_society_noble.title: Court and Nobility
primer.ind_p_society_noble.text: You were born into a noble family. Under the sultans the nobles are amirs – Turks, Afghans and Persians – who receive an iqta for their service: the right to collect a district's taxes and feed their cavalry from them. Hindu rajas and Rajput chiefs hold hill forts, in Vijayanagara the nayakas are commanders with lands, and under Akbar nobles receive ranks called mansabs. At court betel is offered, Persian is spoken, and nobles ride out on elephants.
primer.ind_p_birth.title: Birth
primer.ind_p_birth.text: A midwife, the dai, delivers the baby, and for some ten days the house is considered impure: mother and child live apart. Among Hindus the father touches the baby's lips with honey and ghee, an astrologer casts a horoscope, and on the eleventh or twelfth day the child is named. Around six months the baby is fed rice for the first time. Among Muslims the call to prayer is whispered into the newborn's ear, and on the seventh day a goat is sacrificed and the baby's head shaved – the aqiqa.
primer.ind_p_childhood.title: Childhood
primer.ind_p_childhood.text: At two or three a child's head is shaved, and the first haircut is celebrated by the whole family. Almost all children work from an early age: herding cattle, carrying water, helping at the loom – a trade is inherited from the father. Boys of Brahmin, Kshatriya and Vaishya families undergo upanayana: they receive the sacred thread and go to study with a teacher. Muslim boys go to the maktab to learn the Quran by heart. Girls learn at home, and are often betrothed very young.
primer.ind_p_home.title: Clay and Thatch
primer.ind_p_home.text: A village house has clay walls under a thatched or tiled roof, around an inner courtyard. Every day the floor is smeared with a mix of clay and cow dung, which keeps it clean and keeps insects away. People sleep on a charpai, a wooden frame strung with woven rope; food is cooked on a clay hearth, and water kept in copper and clay pots. In the south the woman of the house draws a pattern in rice flour at the threshold every morning, and a sacred tulsi plant grows in the yard.
primer.ind_p_food.title: Rice, Dal and Ghee
primer.ind_p_food.text: In the south and in Bengal people eat rice with fish and vegetables; in the north, flatbreads of wheat or millet. Every day there is dal made of lentils and other pulses, curds and clarified butter, ghee, with spices – pepper, ginger, turmeric, cardamom. Many Hindus, and all Jains, eat no meat. Ibn Battuta praised khichri, rice cooked with mung beans, and at court they serve sambusa pastries, pilaf and sweets. Chilli peppers will only be brought by the Portuguese in the sixteenth century.
primer.ind_p_clothes.title: Dhoti and Sari
primer.ind_p_clothes.text: Hindus regard unstitched cloth as the purest: men wrap a dhoti around the hips and throw a scarf over the shoulders, women wear the sari with a short blouse, the choli. Muslims wear stitched clothes – a long robe called the jama, trousers and a turban – and at court the rajas adopt them too. Almost everything is cotton, and Bengal muslin is so fine that a length of it can be drawn through a ring. Women wear bangles, and a tilak mark is placed on the forehead.
primer.ind_p_faith.title: Many Faiths
primer.ind_p_faith.text: Most people are Hindus, the rulers are usually Muslims, and alongside them live Jains and the last Buddhists. The faiths don't only quarrel; they also meet: Muslims and Hindus alike visit the Sufi saints. Muin ad-Din Chishti lies buried at Ajmer, Nizam ad-Din Auliya at Delhi, and qawwali is sung at their tombs. In the fifteenth century the weaver Kabir taught that God is one for Hindu and Muslim alike, and Guru Nanak (1469–1539) founded the Sikh teaching in the Punjab.
primer.ind_p_faith_hindu.title: Puja and Darshan
primer.ind_p_faith_hindu.text: Your family is Hindu. Every day at home they perform puja, setting a lamp, flowers and sweets before the image of a god. People go to the temple for darshan – to see the god and be seen by him. Some worship Vishnu, others Shiva, others the Great Goddess. Many dream of bathing in the Ganges at Kashi, where death brings liberation. The bhakti poets – Chaitanya in Bengal, Mirabai in Rajasthan – teach that God can simply be loved, without priests.
primer.ind_p_faith_islam.title: Islam in India
primer.ind_p_faith_islam.text: Your family follows Islam. They pray five times a day, go to the congregational mosque on Fridays and fast from dawn to dusk in Ramadan. The law is interpreted by ulama of the Hanafi school. In Delhi stands the Quwwat al-Islam mosque, built, as its inscription says, from the material of 27 demolished temples. Many Muslims descend from Indians who embraced Islam, often through the Sufis. And the wealthy go on the hajj by sea, from the ports of Gujarat to Jeddah.
primer.ind_p_faith_jain.title: The Jain Path
primer.ind_p_faith_jain.text: Your family is Jain. The first law is ahimsa, doing no harm to any living thing: no meat, no eating after sunset lest you swallow an insect, and for many no root vegetables either. Monks sweep the path before them with a small broom and cover their mouths with cloth, and Digambara monks go naked. The most important festival is Paryushana, days of fasting and repentance. Jain merchants build marble temples on Mount Abu and Shatrunjaya, and in 1583 the monk Hiravijaya spoke with Akbar.
primer.ind_p_faith_buddhist.title: The Last Buddhists
primer.ind_p_faith_buddhist.text: Your family keeps the faith of the Buddha, which was born in these very lands. But around 1200 Bakhtiyar Khalji's troops ravaged the great monasteries of Nalanda and Vikramashila, the monks fled to Tibet and Nepal, and the teaching all but vanished from India. Small communities remain in Bengal, especially around Chittagong. Many customs have blended with Hindu ones, but you will still hear of the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha – the three jewels.
primer.ind_p_work.title: Tanka and Hundi
primer.ind_p_work.text: Sultan Iltutmish began minting the silver tanka, with copper jitals for small change; later Sher Shah will introduce the rupee. Within a jati, a trade passes from father to son. Gujarat cotton and Bengal muslin travel to Aden, Hormuz and Malacca, and Arabian horses come back. Grain moves along the roads with Banjara caravans – thousands of oxen at a time. Merchants send money by hundi, bills of exchange honoured in any large city.
primer.ind_p_place.title: Land of the Monsoon
primer.ind_p_place.text: Hindustan is immense: in the north the plains of the Ganges and Yamuna with wheat and rice, in the west the Thar Desert, in the south the Deccan plateau and green coasts where pepper grows. Spring brings scorching heat and the hot loo wind; summer brings the monsoon, and the rivers flood. Every region has its own language – Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Telugu, Tamil. But everywhere you find the same things: a well, a temple or mosque, a market and a field.
primer.ind_p_place_delhi.title: The Seven Delhis
primer.ind_p_place_delhi.text: Delhi stands on the Yamuna, and every great sultan builds a city of his own: Alauddin built Siri, the Tughluqs Tughlaqabad with its massive walls, Firuz Shah Firozabad, where he brought an ancient pillar of King Ashoka. Above them all rises the Qutb Minar, more than seventy metres tall. At the tomb of the saint Nizam ad-Din, qawwali is sung day and night. In spring dust storms sweep the city; in summer the heat is crushing. Under the Lodis and the Mughals the court often lives in Agra.
primer.ind_p_place_vijayanagara.title: Among the Boulders
primer.ind_p_place_vijayanagara.text: The capital of Vijayanagara spreads among giant granite boulders on the Tungabhadra River, which people cross in round wicker boats. The Virupaksha temple towers over bazaars where, according to the Portuguese visitor Paes, diamonds and pearls were sold right in the street, and the Vitthala temple has a chariot carved of stone. Every autumn, at the Mahanavami festival, the king reviews parades of elephants. After 1565 the city lies in ruins, but life in the surrounding land goes on.
primer.ind_p_place_bengal.title: Land of Rivers
primer.ind_p_place_bengal.text: Bengal is the land where the Ganges splits into hundreds of channels. People travel by boat more than on foot, eat rice with fish, and tigers roam the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans. Sonargaon weaves its famous muslin. Stone is scarce, so mosques and temples are built of brick with delicate terracotta carving; the Adina mosque at Pandua is one of the largest in India. In the sixteenth century Chaitanya sang and danced in ecstasy at Nabadwip, and the Portuguese appeared at Chittagong.
primer.ind_p_place_gujarat.title: Cambay's Two Arms
primer.ind_p_place_gujarat.text: The Portuguese writer Tome Pires said that Cambay stretches out two arms: with the right it reaches toward Aden, with the left toward Malacca. Gujarat's ports are full of ships, weavers print patterns on cotton, and the craftsmen of Cambay grind beads of agate and carnelian. Ahmedabad has its Friday Mosque of 1424 with some two hundred and sixty pillars, and in this dry land people build stepwells several storeys deep. Jain and Bania merchants are the richest people in the land.
primer.ind_p_law.title: Qazi and Panchayat
primer.ind_p_law.text: Cases involving Muslims and the state are judged by a qazi under sharia, but the sultan also holds his own court, often far harsher: Muhammad bin Tughluq was feared for his cruel executions. Hindus more often turn to their own people: the community council, the panchayat, rules on marriage, inheritance and who is to be cast out of the jati. Disputed cases may still be settled by ordeal, by fire or water. For many the worst fate is not prison but expulsion from the community.
primer.ind_p_health.title: Vaidyas and Hakims
primer.ind_p_health.text: Hindu healers, vaidyas, follow Ayurveda: illness is an imbalance of the body's three humours, corrected with herbs, diet and oils. Muslim hakims practise Greek-Arabic medicine, and Firuz Shah opened a hospital in Delhi that treated people free of charge. The worst afflictions are cholera, fevers after the monsoon, and smallpox, revered as the goddess Shitala and appeased with offerings. And famine: in years of crop failure whole villages die out.
primer.ind_p_women.title: A Woman's Life
primer.ind_p_women.text: Marriages are arranged by parents within the jati, and a girl is often betrothed very young, moving to her husband's home when she is older. She lives in his large family under her mother-in-law's authority. Her own property is her stridhan, jewellery and gifts that remain hers. In the higher castes a widow may not remarry; in many other communities she may. Yet there were women rulers: Sultan Razia, Rani Durgavati, who fell in battle in 1564, and Chand Bibi, defender of Ahmadnagar.
primer.ind_p_women_islam.title: Purdah
primer.ind_p_women_islam.text: In noble and well-off Muslim families women live in purdah, 'behind the curtain': in the women's quarters of the house, the zenana, going out veiled or in a palanquin. Poor women who work in the fields and markets cannot afford such a life. At marriage the groom pledges the bride her mahr, under sharia a daughter inherits half her brother's share, and divorce is possible for either side. Many noble Hindus of the north adopt seclusion as well.
primer.ind_p_women_hindu.title: Vows and Customs
primer.ind_p_women_hindu.text: Women keep vows, vrats, fasting for the health of husband and children; they water the tulsi and lead the household rites. In the north married women veil their faces with the end of the sari before elders. A widow of the higher castes wears white and lives modestly. Occasionally, more often in Rajput and noble families, a widow mounted her husband's funeral pyre – sati. The custom was never universal and many condemned it; Muhammad bin Tughluq required permission for it, and Akbar forbade forcing anyone into it.
primer.ind_p_leisure.title: Festivals and Games
primer.ind_p_leisure.text: In spring, at Holi, people throw coloured powder; in autumn, at Diwali, thousands of clay lamps are lit; at Dussehra Rama's victory is acted out. Muslims celebrate the two Eids with feasts and new clothes. People play chess, shatranj, and chaupar, throwing pieces on a cross-shaped board. Wrestlers grapple in the sand, and nobles play chaugan, polo on horseback – Aibak died falling from his horse in a match. The poet Amir Khusrau, they say, invented qawwali.
primer.ind_p_knowledge.title: Sanskrit and Persian
primer.ind_p_knowledge.text: Brahmin scholars write in Sanskrit, the sultans' courts speak and write Persian, and ordinary people compose songs in Hindi, Bengali and Telugu. In the south people write on palm leaves; in the north paper spreads ever wider. Firuz Shah opened a madrasa by the Hauz Khas tank. In Kerala, around 1400, the mathematician Madhava of Sangamagrama found infinite series for pi, centuries before the Europeans. But few people can read.
primer.ind_p_war.title: Elephants and Horses
primer.ind_p_war.text: The main strength of Indian armies is the war elephant, and the sultans also have Turkish horse archers. Good horses are scarce in India: they are shipped from Arabia and Persia, and the southern kings pay fortunes for them. Rajputs hold out in hill forts – Chittor, Ranthambore – and prefer death to surrender. In 1526 at Panipat Babur first showed India the power of cannon and muskets. A village suffers from any army, its own or the enemy's.
